prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms opened a new regime of precision frequency measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B014 as a single-achievement prize for Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange I can state the scientific case more sharply than before. The decisive idea is that at the magic wavelength the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so a very large number of neutral atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed, while the atom number beats down quantum projection noise. That is a statement about how to control a quantum system, not merely a better ruler, and it is what separates this from the frequency comb (a ruler that counts optical cycles, 2005) and from single-ion control (one quantum system, 2012). The result has been reproduced and surpassed across several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) with mutual agreement near 1e-18, which is the robustness test I always apply, and it has already delivered new physics: gravitational redshift over millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, many-body and collective effects in the clock ensemble, and bounds on drifting constants. I read the citation as rewarding the invention and its realisation at record performance, not the SI redefinition, which is a metrological decision that follows from the physics and does not condition it.
statement.case_against: The reservations that all six of us carry remain real. The lattice clock sits in a lineage already prized in 1989, 2005 and 2012, so a sceptic will call it a third prize for one field; the redefinition of the second is not yet decided; and Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names. The chair is also right that part of the convergence on B014 is members moving toward the safest option, and I include myself in that: I ranked B009 first in my opening ballot and now rank B014 first. I have tried to test that by asking whether I would still defend B014 if no one else did, and I would, on the Lamb-Dicke argument and the multi-laboratory reproduction. What I cannot dismiss is that a clock is an enabling instrument whose full scientific payoff (geodesy, dark-matter and constant searches) is still largely prospective, which is Danielsson's point and a fair one.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B021 (IceCube) because nature supplied a diffuse flux nobody predicted and the clock is a measurement of a world we already knew, and he suggests the clock can wait for the SI redefinition at no cost.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument distinction seriously and I have changed my reading of B021 because of it: in round 1 I said source identification was partial and left it there, but you and Pearce are right that the prize would be for the secure diffuse flux and the technique, not for a source catalogue, so I now list B021 among my alternatives. I still differ on two points. First, the lattice clock is not only an instrument: gravitational redshift across centimetres and many-body clock physics are results about nature. Second, waiting is not free in the way you suggest, because the prize is for the demonstrated science, not for a CGPM schedule, and tying it to the redefinition would make a scientific award hostage to a metrological timetable. I cannot judge the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA credit and would defer to you and Pearce, but I agree with Olsson that Spiering should stay in any IceCube credit. What would move me toward B021 is an expert assessment that KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD independently corroborate the flux.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B016 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new class of matter defined by topology, argues the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and not the Z2 invariant and HgTe experiment, and asks whether I should step back from B009.
responses.response: I accept his argument that the Z2 invariant, time-reversal-protected edge states and the HgTe measurement are physically distinct from the 2016 work, and that is why B016 remains my first alternative and the conceptually deepest entry on the list. My remaining obstacle is the one he names himself: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is outside the three names and Zhang's death makes that irreparable, so I do not think it is cleaner than a two-name clock prize. A citation that names the theory and the first observation without claiming the whole field is defensible, so if the committee decides the credit gap is tolerable I would support B016 over any weaker alternative. On his question about B009: yes, I will step back. I will take no part in advocating or ballot-ranking B009, and in this round it is not in my configuration or my alternatives. I would also ask the committee to read my opening first place for B009 as a field-proximity signal and not as evidence for the candidate.

responses.point: Kroll supports B014 as a new measurement technique with a clean invention-plus-realisation attribution, proposes a single-achievement prize, and asks whether I would support B008 as a fallback if B014 fails to carry the committee.
responses.response: I agree on the single-achievement framing, because a B014 plus second-part configuration cannot fit the three-person limit without cutting the clock pair. On B008 as a fallback, I would not be a strong advocate: Wineland's 2012 prize already covers much of the ion-gate foundation, and the credited set splits a compound field (Blatt versus Bloch), so I rank it below B016 and B021 as a fallback. Given our shared WACQT and Chalmers ties, I would also ask that neither of us carries weight on B009, and I note we agree that it should wait. I share his point that the citation should rest on invention and realisation and not promise geodesy or dark-matter applications, which are still mostly projected.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B014 as a genuine conceptual step (magic wavelength plus Lamb-Dicke regime), says she may be too fond of it as a neighbouring field, and is asked by the chair whether she would defend the distinction from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes.
responses.response: I answer the chair's question in my own voice and with her argument. The one-sentence distinction is that the comb counts optical cycles, ion control manipulates one quantum system, and the lattice clock reaches its stability by interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms with the dominant systematic shift cancelled by design. I think that distinction can be stated in a citation and defended to a colleague who sees one field honoured three times, though not without some residual doubt. On priority, I recall that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal (around 2001-2003) preceded the strontium lattice demonstrations and the later Ye-group 1e-18 comparisons, but this is recollection and I have not checked dates against papers. Since she is closest to the field, I would ask her to confirm that history, and the roles of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto, before the final ballot, as Olsson also asks.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved B014 to the head of his configuration after reading the opening ballots, leaves atomic clocks to colleagues, and notes Olsson's point that Spiering should stay in any IceCube credit.
responses.response: I appreciate his candour about moving toward B014, and I think the right test is the one the chair proposes: whether the reasons survive when counts are removed. For me they do, on the physics and the reproduction. I also agree with him and with Olsson that a two-name IceCube credit would weaken the attribution, which is one reason I do not fix on B021 this year even though I now list it as an alternative. I defer to him on astroparticle facts. I would ask the chair to record that the committee's agreement on B014 comes in part from members moving toward it, and that the final ballot should therefore weigh the three shared reservations and not the count.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a discovery in the sense of the statutes or as a metrological invention whose full impact depends on the undecided redefinition of the second.

The exact priority chronology among Katori (magic-wavelength proposal), the first lattice demonstrations, Ye's group and Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups is recalled and not checked against papers; I would want an expert check before the final ballot.
Whether the distinction from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I find defensible, will persuade the whole committee and the wider community.
I cannot judge B016 or B021 on attribution or on independent confirmation beyond what colleagues have said, and I defer to Eriksson, Danielsson and Pearce on those.
statement.conflict_note: Specific connection: I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a theorist in the Chalmers superconducting-circuit community, with close professional ties to circuit QED groups. In response to Eriksson's question I will step back from B009 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) and, to a lesser extent, B008: I do not advocate for or rank either in this round, and my opening first place for B009 should be discounted. I also share the Chalmers environment with Olsson and Mehlig. I know of no specific conflict for B014, B016 or B021.
